disease.mechanism: Loss-of-function. Deficiency of glucocerebrosidase (GCase) impairs lysosomal degradation of glucosylceramide, which accumulates in macrophages, forming 'Gaucher cells' in spleen, liver, and bone marrow. This causes hepatosplenomegaly, cytopenias, and bone disease (type 1, non-neuronopathic) or additional neurological involvement (types 2-3).
disease.autotac_rationale: NOT eligible. Gaucher disease is a loss-of-function enzyme deficiency — GCase is deficient, not accumulated. The correct route is enzyme replacement therapy (restore GCase), not protein degradation.
disease.prevalence: ~1 in 40,000-60,000 general population; ~1 in 850 in Ashkenazi Jewish population (commonly cited) — UNVERIFIED exact figure this session
disease.age_of_onset: Type 1: variable, childhood to adulthood; Type 2: infancy (severe); Type 3: childhood (neuronopathic)

approved_treatments.mechanism_correct: Recombinant human glucocerebrosidase that replaces the deficient enzyme, restoring glucosylceramide degradation. Administered intravenously. This is the definitive disease-modifying therapy for type 1 Gaucher disease.
approved_treatments.note: NOTE: imiglucerase is a recombinant glycoprotein enzyme (~55 kDa), NOT a small molecule — molecular weight and PubChem CID are not applicable (MW/CID fields left 0 to avoid fabrication).

investigational: Substrate reduction therapy: eliglustat (oral, glucosylceramide synthase inhibitor) and miglustat
Gene therapy (AAV-mediated GBA1 delivery, preclinical/early clinical)

disease.human_summary: Gaucher disease is the most common lysosomal storage disorder, an autosomal recessive deficiency of glucocerebrosidase. It causes glucocerebroside accumulation in macrophages, leading to enlarged spleen/liver, low blood counts, and bone disease. Enzyme replacement therapy is the standard disease-modifying treatment for the non-neuronopathic form.
